title: How to Clean Brake Dust Off Alloys (Without Damaging Them)
meta_description: Why alloys go brown, why strong acid wheel cleaners are risky, and the safe way to clean brake dust off your wheels at home, step by step.
excerpt: Brake dust is mostly iron, which is why alloys turn brown and a quick rinse doesn't shift it. Here's the safe way to clean it off, and when it isn't dirt at all.

keywords: how to clean brake dust off alloys

faq.q: Why do my alloy wheels go brown?
faq.a: Brake dust contains tiny particles of iron from the discs. Once they're on the wheel and get wet, they rust, which turns silver alloys grey, then brown.

faq.q: Can I use an acid wheel cleaner on alloys?
faq.a: It's best avoided. Strong acid cleaners can stain or dull polished, diamond-cut and chrome finishes, and get under damaged lacquer. A non-acid wheel cleaner and an iron fallout remover do the job more safely.
An iron fallout remover. It reacts with the bonded iron particles, usually turning purple as it works, so they rinse away without hard scrubbing.

faq.q: Why won't the brown come off my wheels?
faq.a: If it's under the lacquer, bubbling or powdery, it's corrosion rather than dirt, and no cleaner will remove it. That needs a wheel refurbisher.

Alloys gone brown? That's brake dust. It's full of tiny iron particles from the discs, and once they get wet they rust onto the wheel, which is why a quick rinse doesn't shift them.

The fix isn't a stronger cleaner. Strong acid wheel cleaners can stain polished and diamond-cut finishes. A non-acid wheel cleaner, soft brushes and an iron fallout remover get the brown off safely.

Our new guide explains why alloys go brown, the safe way to clean them at home, and how to tell when it's damage rather than dirt.
